article.articleHeadline: Even with hundreds of millions of dollars in aid, the spread of Ebola couldn't be contained... The disease-control frontline is short of personnel and equipment - Sisa Journal
article.articleSummary:
- Six months into the Democratic Republic of Congo's second-largest Ebola outbreak, transmission remains uncontained despite hundreds of millions in aid. In Ituri, Haut-Uele and North Kivu provinces, frontline responders report severe shortages of personnel, medical supplies, and equipment, with some staff unpaid and ambulances running on fuel shortages. Healthcare workers treat suspected cases without adequate materials. MSF warns that despite large funding, many frontline teams lack gear and salaries, hampering containment. Surveillance gaps persist: despite resource allocations, several areas are neglected, and about two-thirds of Ebola deaths in the past month occurred outside treatment centers, delaying detection and isolation. Only 9% of MSF-treated patients were previously identified 
- Six months into the Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, transmission continues and expands to new areas. Women and girls make up more than 53% of cases; among 15–17-year-olds, girls represent two-thirds of cases and 60% of deaths. More than 2,280 children have been orphaned or separated. Sixteen nurseries provide protection services. Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warns the outbreak remains out of control more than six months after it was first declared, citing attacks on healthcare workers, delays in staff salaries, and a shortage of resources. The Kinshasa-based daily report confirms ongoing transmission in the DRC as of 17 November 2026. - Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains uncontrolled, Africa CDC Director Kassaye said on November 15 in Ethiopia. The outbreak, first declared May 15 in DR Congo, has surpassed 11,000 cumulative cases and 5,400 deaths. It has spread to eight provinces and 67 health zones, with new weekly cases still about 400–500. If not brought under effective control, this wave could become the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. article.articleHeadline: 1918 - Spanish flu: government responds to criticisms by Corumbá's health inspector.
article.articleSummary: Spanish flu drives a sanitary barrier decision in Mato Grosso, Brazil. In a 16 November 1918 letter, Governor Dom Aquino Corrêa responds to Corumbá port health inspector Gastão de Oliveira, justifying a sanitary barrier at Amolar to isolate Cuiabá from contagion detected in the city. The government emphasizes urgent sanitary measures for the south while protecting the less-developed north, orders a medical post at Amolar, and mandates five-day observation of all vessels from that port, with arrivals showing illness to return due to lack of hospital facilities. Acknowledging the absence of a federal sanitary service in Cuiabá, the policy aims to reassure the populace, prevent infected individuals from entering immune populations, and maintain morale during the epidemic. Source: A Cruz (Cuiabá), 24/11/1918.

article.articleHeadline: Butantan Institute Creates Center to Research Treatments for the Sequelae of Chikungunya, Dengue, and Zika
article.articleSummary: Butantan Institute in São Paulo, Brazil, announces creation of the Center of Technology in Arboviruses (CeTA) to study long-lasting symptoms after infections by chikungunya, dengue, Zika, and yellow fever. The project will investigate persistent inflammatory, neurological, and joint manifestations to identify molecular targets for new therapies. Using artificial intelligence to mine research data for patterns explaining symptom persistence, the team will pinpoint molecules that could serve as therapeutic targets. Candidate treatments will be evaluated in three-dimensional human cell–based models, reducing reliance on animal testing. Leveraging existing infrastructure from a 2016 project, CeTA aims in five years to validate at least three molecular targets and advance two treatment biologics or vaccines to advanced preclinical testing. Funded by Fapesp, CeTA partners include the Ragon Institute (affiliated with MIT, Harvard, Mass General Brigham) and CNPEM in Campinas, São Paulo.

article.articleHeadline: Vaccination of pregnant women in Goiás reduces severe cases of the virus.
article.articleSummary: Vaccination of pregnant women against Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in Goiás, Brazil, began in November 2025 and reached 85% coverage, above the 80% goal. A preliminary SES-GO study links maternal RSV vaccination to fewer severe SRAG cases, reduced ICU admissions, and less invasive ventilation among infants, especially those under six months. The analysis shows a 60.6% reduction in projected RSV-related SRAG cases in children under one year. ICU admission rates declined from 46.8% to 37.2% (under six months), 49.3% to 40.4% (under three months), and 43.0% to 32.9% (under one year). Invasive ventilation dropped from 19.2% to 8.9% (under one year); 21.1% to 12.6% (under three months); 20.7% to 9.1% (3–5 months); 13.5% to 6.4% (6–11 months). The composite ICU/ventilation/death indicator fell from 45.6% to 35.7% in under-1-year-olds. Results are preliminary; a full season and potential contributions from nirsevimabe in high-risk groups are noted. Premature infants began receiving nirsevimabe in February 2026.

article.articleSummary: Foz do Iguaçu’s Eastern Region will host a dengue-control mutirão starting Monday, 16 November 2026, through 27 November 2026, as part of the Semana de Mobilização de Combate à Dengue. Coordinated by the Municipal Secretariat of Environment, the operation includes yard cleaning, sweeping, tree pruning, and removal of materials discarded in public spaces to reduce Aedes aegypti breeding sites. A total of 38 dumpsters will be placed at locations across Morumbi, Morumbi II, Portal da Foz, Portal, and other neighborhoods to facilitate disposal of old furniture, construction debris, and similar waste; residents can also submit requests via the e-Ouve app. Concentration of teams is at 8:30 a.m. at Praça 7 de Setembro (Morumbi). The effort supports national Dia D activities and aims to lower dengue, Zika, and chikungunya risks by eliminating standing-water sources.

article.articleHeadline: Salmonella: Association Between Probiotics May Broaden Coverage, Trial Suggests.
article.articleSummary: Multi-strain probiotic combinations broaden Salmonella inhibition in broilers, per an in vitro assay by BioSyn under its Enhanced Integrity Program. Seven probiotic strains were tested against four Salmonella serovars (Mbandaka, Heidelberg, Minnesota, Anatum) and one E. coli isolate from broiler housing, loading surfaces, composting areas, and joints. No single strain inhibited all serovars strongly; combined results yielded high inhibition across pathogens. Of 35 strain–pathogen combos, 14 formed halos and nine showed high inhibition. Yeasts produced the largest halos but did not inhibit S. Heidelberg or E. coli; Lactobacillus acidophilus was active against all five pathogens, though with smaller halos. Halo size and spectrum did not always align. Practically, three-stage probiotic deployment is advised: early hatchery colonization, maintaining microbiota through processing, and rapid re-colonization after dysbiosis or antibiotics. A 2023 study reported resistance in S. Heidelberg and S. Minnesota to third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones in Brazilian broilers.

article.articleHeadline: Global Synthesis Details Foot-and-Mouth Disease Diversity and Heavy
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious transboundary infection of cloven-hoofed livestock and wildlife. A global synthesis of 272 studies (1986–2025) shows FMD virus is an 8.4-kb positive-sense RNA Aphthovirus with seven immunologically distinct serotypes (O, A, C, Asia1, SAT1–SAT3) that lack cross-protection. Serotype C has not been detected since 2004 in Brazil and is presumed extinct; the others remain active with regionally distinct topotypes. In Southeast, Central, and East Asia serotype O dominates (Cathay, SEA, ME-SA), with Cathay linked to swine-adaptation via 3A deletions. In South Asia, O accounts for most outbreaks (India ~92%), while A and Asia1 are less common. Africa shows complex dynamics across East, North, West/Central, and Southern regions, with SAT2 prevalent in Southern Africa. South America has progressed toward elimination through vaccination and movement controls; confirmation of freedom remains challenging. Economic losses total 6.5–21B USD/year in endemic regions, plus ~1.5B USD in disease-free nations; Sub-Saharan Africa losses >2B, with implications for trade and vaccination programs, including potential outbreaks in high-income exporters like Australia.

article.articleHeadline: Ceará hosts the Second Symposium on Infectious and Inflammatory Diseases | Fiocruz Portal
article.articleSummary: II Symposium on Infectious and Inflammatory Diseases will take place in Ceará, Brazil, from November 17–19, 2026. The free in-person event, organized by Fiocruz Ceará, IOC, Rede Translational Fio-Mucosa, TGHN LAC, and URCA, will run 8:30–17:00 Brasília time and gather researchers, health professionals, and students to share advances in infectious and inflammatory diseases. More than 20 speakers from Ceará, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Bahia, Piauí and Espírito Santo will cover antimicrobial resistance, leishmaniasis, leprosy, fungal diseases, geohelminthiases elimination, RNA vaccines, and nanobodies for neglected diseases. The symposium aims to strengthen SUS and regional collaboration, bridging Southeast and Northeast institutions and supporting human resource development. Brazil reported 22,129 new Hansen’s disease cases in 2024, with the country ranking second globally after India. The program includes roundtables, short courses, posters, and closing remarks by Wilson Savino.

article.articleHeadline: Tecpar reinforces the importance of vaccination for the prevention of human rabies.
article.articleSummary: Rabies vaccination in Brazil: the Instituto de Tecnologia do Paraná (Tecpar) was selected in 2025 as the sole public laboratory supplying the human rabies vaccine for the Ministry of Health, via a technology-transfer partnership with Sinovac under the PDP. Rabies is lethal after symptoms but preventable with vaccination and rapid post-exposure prophylaxis; Brazil has only two reported human survivors. The vaccine, available through the SUS, can be given pre-exposure for high-risk professionals or immediately after exposure. Tecpar's move aims to strengthen SUS and reduce import dependence; the vaccine has been registered with China's NMPA, and Anvisa submission will assess quality, safety, efficacy, and Brazilian manufacturing conditions. Transmission occurs through saliva after animal bites, scratches, or mucosal contact; incubation averages ~45 days, with early nonspecific symptoms and later neurologic signs. Dogs and cats are main urban transmitters, but wildlife reservoirs like bats, foxes, saguis, keep transmission ongoing; vigilance remains.

article.articleHeadline: Ministry steps up Ebola awareness, surveillance in Busia
article.articleSummary: Ebola awareness and surveillance have intensified in Busia, Kenya, focusing on Teso North during the 42-day mandatory monitoring toward Ebola-free status, due to end December 23, 2026. Led by the Ministry of Health and the Kenya Red Cross Society, the programme strengthens community awareness, early detection, and prevention along the Northern Corridor border. Target groups include sex workers, long-distance truck drivers, persons with disabilities, women’s groups, youth, the elderly, and religious leaders; chiefs and ward leaders will mobilize residents and facilitate referrals, with herbalists and traditional healers directing danger-sign patients to facilities. No community transmission has been reported; Kenyan cases are linked to infections from the Democratic Republic of Congo. A 30-day action roadmap, 'Together for a Healthy and Safe Teso North,' guides activities, and officials warn against misconceptions such as chang'aa immunity.

article.articleHeadline: Congo-Kinshasa: The fear of Ebola leads to a drop in hospital attendance.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus, Bundibugyo strain, in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri) triggers a sharp drop in hospital attendance as fear grows. In Bukavu and Sud-Kivu, clinics report declines since April 2026—from around 20 consultations per day at Kalunga health center to about 5, with some days no patients. Residents increasingly self-medicate, citing fear of isolation, stigma, and dying alone in treatment centers, followed by bereavement without family rites. Experts stress this is a social protection response to a polycrisis that includes ongoing conflict, COVID-19 trauma, extreme poverty, eroding trust in institutions, and infodemic. Two Ebola cases have been confirmed in the Miti-Murhesa health zone (Kabare, South Kivu). The outbreak reframes hospitals as spaces of danger rather than refuge during this crisis.

article.articleHeadline: Contipharma presents the first all-in-one saliva test for malaria diagnosis.
article.articleSummary: Liège-based Contipharma unveils Smart, the first all-in-one saliva test to screen for malaria, to be presented on Monday at Medica in Düsseldorf, Germany. The device combines sampling, analysis, and result interpretation in a single unit, replacing finger-prick blood collection, sample transfer, and laboratory analysis. By simplifying the process and reducing error risk, it targets children and communities in remote, malaria-endemic areas. The test is currently being validated by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo, a country severely affected by malaria. CEO Bernard Delhez notes Kinshasa was chosen because policy decisions on malaria are made there, and eradicating malaria requires identifying the invisible reservoir on the ground, where people live, not only the sick.

article.articleHeadline: Congo-Kinshasa: Butembo civil society warns of the risks associated with the strike by healthcare providers involved in the Ebola response.
article.articleSummary: As of 16 November 2026, civil society in Butembo, North Kivu, Congo-Kinshasa warns that a strike by healthcare providers involved in the Ebola response is disrupting care at Ebola treatment and transit centers in Butembo and Katwa health zones. The workers are demanding two months of back salaries, a revision of the salary scale, and improvements to working conditions and equipment. The civil society calls on authorities to intervene swiftly to resolve the dispute, fearing consequences for patient management and ongoing Ebola outbreak control. They warn that care gaps could lead to deterioration of patients admitted in facilities and could complicate outbreak control, especially as some contacts remain untraceable and the epidemic remains not fully controlled. At the time of reporting, authorities' response had not been obtained.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: "Right now, it's difficult for everyone to gauge the situation."
article.articleSummary: An interview on the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo Ebola outbreak centers on Ituri and North Kivu, with Goma at the epicenter. In about five and a half months the outbreak has cost over 5,000 lives. Transmission is driven by mild early symptoms that mimic malaria, keeping patients infectious as they interact with teachers, drivers, traders, and clergy. Traditional caregiving and funerals—where the deceased are washed, combed, and touched—fuel spread, despite knowledge of protective measures. A colleague recounts 46 relatives dying in his family; his daughter survived but his brother did not. The response is criticized as “Ebola business,” with rapid foreign teams and booming isolation centers seeding distrust in a region ravaged by conflict, displacement, and poverty. Rwanda shut and then reopened its border; strict contact tracing and quarantines are emphasized to curb cross-border transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: a virus survivor, this doctor has resumed his practice with patients.
article.articleSummary: DRC Ebola outbreak persists in Butembo, North Kivu, driven by Bundibugyo ebolavirus; about 11,000 infections and 5,400 deaths, making it the second-deadliest on record, with 3,031 survivors. Dr. Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga, a 30-year-old physician at Katwa Hospital in Butembo, survived after a 13-day inpatient course of supportive care for dehydration and organ stress. He likely contracted the virus from a patient where protective measures were inadequate. Early symptoms included a bitter taste, headaches, and malaise, progressing to vomiting and diarrhea; diagnosis was delayed because Butembo lacks rapid testing, with samples sent 54 km to Beni, taking 48–72 hours. After recovery, stigma persisted; his family kept distance for 21 days (the incubation period). He has written a book and returned to work, hoping to curb transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Developments in obesity treatment and Ebola and measles outbreaks in 2026 at this stage.
article.articleSummary: Obesity therapies: Lilly disclosed Phase 2 data for an experimental obesity regimen combining Eloralintatide and Tirzepatide (full results not yet published) at ObesityWeek 2026. Novo Nordisk real-world data show patients taking the daily Wegovy achieving an average 6.2% weight loss over three months, signaling ongoing competition in oral obesity treatments. Outbreaks: Africa CDC says the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains uncontrolled after six months, hampered by attacks on health workers, unpaid salaries, and resource shortages. In the United States, measles persists in Pennsylvania, with 1,542 cases across 46 counties and 305 hospitalizations; seven deaths this year occurred in an unvaccinated Montour County resident. The Wall Street Journal notes the US no longer meets measles elimination status due to ongoing transmission. Pharma policy: CVS Health suggests GLP-1 inhibitors priced under $350/month could enable insurer breakeven, though current prices remain high. FDA declined approval for Ivonisumab from Samat Therapeutics for lung cancer. In China, Pfizer and Innovent Biologics GLP-1s will be covered by national health insurance for type 2 diabetes from Jan 1, boosting competition in diabetes and obesity markets.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Tshopo: The Red Cross is the only on-the-ground actor in Bafwasende - ACP
article.articleSummary: As of November 16, 2026, Ebola remains active in the Bafwasende territory of the Democratic Republic of Congo, 264 km east of Kisangani. The Red Cross is the sole on-the-ground responder, with volunteers conducting house-to-house, market, and public-area sensitization against Ebola. Hospitals in Bafwasende are reported emptied, and residents fear for their fate as humanitarian workers and other technical-financial partners have withdrawn amid persistent threats and even fatal accusations tied to the outbreak. Jean-Marie Aluka, president of the DRC Red Cross in Bafwasende, says he is receiving death threats; volunteers also face threats during outreach and funeral activities. Jeanne Magbolo, a Red Cross educator, notes hostility from groups opposing the response, risking the lives of those speaking about Ebola in the area. No case counts, laboratory confirmation, or infection source are provided in the report.

article.articleHeadline: Barrick's Kibali reinforces health screenings after Ebola cases
article.articleSummary: Two Ebola cases in the surrounding community near Kibali, the joint Barrick-AngloGold Ashanti mine in the Democratic Republic of Congo, have prompted Barrick to temporarily demobilise non-essential personnel at the Kibali site. There have been two fatalities from the confirmed community cases. No employees or contractors have been identified as exposed; mining operations continue normally. As a precaution, Kibali has reinforced health screening and monitoring, strengthened emergency response arrangements, and offers confidential medical assessment and follow-up. The move underscores proactive public health measures amid an ongoing outbreak risk, with the surrounding community monitored for further cases. Kibali produced 203,000 oz of gold in Q3, at an all-in sustaining cost of $1,430/oz. The mine is 45% Barrick, 45% AngloGold Ashanti, 10% SOKIMO. The op-ed cited discusses Ebola’s potential regional economic disruption through quarantines, border closures, and site shutdowns.

The parliament urges residents to seek examination at authorized health facilities, avoid self-medication and rumors, and not delay care. Health professionals can determine whether a case is Ebola; when detected and managed promptly in appropriate centers, recovery chances are real. Adherence to prevention and care measures is crucial to curb the outbreak in the Beni region.

article.articleHeadline: WHO: Among confirmed tuberculosis cases in North Korea, the rate of drug susceptibility testing is 1.9%, while the world average is 85%.
article.articleSummary: WHO reports that in North Korea, among bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis cases last year, only 1.9% underwent rifampicin resistance testing (DST), far below the global average of 85%. North Korea is among 30 high-burden countries with DST below 50%, with Mozambique at 2.2% and the Democratic Republic of Congo at 30%; by contrast, 22 of the 30 high-burden countries achieve 80%+ DST. Rifampicin testing is crucial to selecting appropriate therapy, since rifampicin resistance necessitates second-line drugs. Globally, 8.4 million people were newly diagnosed with TB last year; 59% received WHO-recommended rapid diagnostics at first testing, and about 370,000 RR-TB cases were estimated, of which 155,333 (42%) were treated. Cure rates are ~90% for drug-susceptible TB vs ~70% for RR-TB. North Korea’s incidence estimates are under review and excluded from national maps, but NK remains among high-burden countries and contributed to over half of the global increase in TB preventive therapy among household contacts aged 5+.

article.articleHeadline: North Kivu: more than 450 cholera cases and 82 deaths recorded in.
article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreak intensifies in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, centered in North Kivu’s Masisi and Walikale territories, with secondary transmission in parts of South Kivu. Since the outbreak was officially declared on 19 September, the Katoyi health zone has recorded more than 450 cases and 82 deaths. Two additional cholera deaths were reported overnight Sunday–Monday, 16 November 2026, in Bitoyi and Kirambo health centers (Ufamandu II groupement, Masisi). The epidemic has spread to Kibua and Itebero in Walikale, and hundreds of cases are reported in Ziralo, South Kivu, including many displaced persons. Response is hindered by insecurity and logistical constraints; a 17-carton batch of IV fluids for severely dehydrated patients has been blocked for about two weeks roughly 40 km from the affected area amid clashes in Masisi. North Kivu’s Division of Health had not yet commented at publication.

article.articleHeadline: Tuberculosis Care Delays Exceed Acceptable Limits Across Seven High-Burden
article.articleSummary: TB care delays across seven high-burden countries exceed the conventional 30-day threshold for timely TB management. Pooled mean patient delay is 24.65 days (95% CI 21.19–28.10) and treatment delay 8.96 days (95% CI 7.64–10.28). Bangladesh records the highest diagnosis delay at 93.50 days (95% CI 55.13–131.87); India shows the longest patient delay (129.33 days, 95% CI 26.32–232.35) and treatment delay (149.67 days, 95% CI 74.54–224.79). Across 79 studies (n=6,477,766 participants), the seven-country analysis excludes the Democratic Republic of Congo due to no eligible data and accounts for about 63% of global TB burden. Substantial heterogeneity and publication bias were detected; COVID-19 had heterogeneous impacts on delays across settings. The authors call policy action to reduce both patient and health-system delays to interrupt transmission, drawing on data from PUBMED/Scopus/Embase/Web of Science using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model.

article.articleHeadline: Del Val urges vigilance to prevent another potential infectious outbreak.
article.articleSummary: As of 16 November 2026, virologist Margarita del Val argues for vigilance and proactive surveillance to prevent outbreaks. She notes post-COVID shifts: faster international cooperation, stronger health systems, and a shift from reactive to anticipatory responses. In Spain, vector-borne risks include tiger mosquito spreading dengue with cases in the Balearic Islands, and West Nile virus circulating in parts of Andalusia since 2020 (no vaccine yet; control via larvicides). Monkeypox re-emerged in Spain in 2022 and surged again in 2024 due to a new variant; vaccines essential. Avian influenza remains mostly animal-to-human with limited human transmission. Hantavirus outbreaks linked to a Canary Islands cruise prompted international mobilization. The most dire threat is Ebola Bundibugyo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with over 10,000 cases and export to France; five vaccines in development, with trials begun in 57 days. Lessons: readiness, vaccine development timelines under 100 days, and understanding 30 virus families.

article.articleHeadline: Quarantine Headquarters issues a risk advisory for highly pathogenic avian influenza (AI)
article.articleSummary: Nov 13, 2026: Korea's Animal and Plant Quarantine Agency (APQA) issued a High-Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) risk advisory as domestic poultry outbreaks rise and wild birds test positive for H5N1 and H5N9. Since Oct 12, HPAI antigens were detected in wild birds at Suncheon Bay, with a total of 10 detections to date, and six poultry-farm outbreaks: Yeoncheon and Yeoju (Gyeonggi Province) layer farms; Jangheung (Jeollanam-do) fattening duck farm; Ganghwa (Incheon) layer farm; Jincheon (Chungcheongbuk-do) breeding duck farm; and Paju (Gyeonggi) quail farm. Migratory-bird tracking shows a mallard moving south from Baicheng, Jilin, China, arriving in Uljin, North Gyeongsang, by Nov 7. In Japan, HP AI antigens were detected in wild birds/environments in Akita, Hokkaido, Kagoshima, with suspected cases in Kyoto (200,000-layer) and Chiba (40,000-layer) farms. Measures include two-stage farm-vehicle disinfection, PPE and dedicated footwear, closing back doors without anterooms, entry disinfection, hand hygiene, and intensified central inspections.

article.articleHeadline: Is water from a reverse osmosis purifier drinkable? Field test in 20 households: multiple samples exceed the standard for total bacterial colony counts.
article.articleSummary: Beijing-based field test of 20 households with under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) purifiers found drinking water often exceeds microbial standards. The study, covering brands including AO Smith, Angel, and Midea, collected two sample sets per household: A (daily-use water after typical flushing) and B (after disinfection with a 5-minute flush). Among 20 A samples, 14 exceeded the GB 5749 2022 limit for total bacterial colonies (100 CFU/mL), with a maximum of 3000 CFU/mL; 1 sample showed total coliforms (2 MPN/100 mL) and no E. coli was detected. In 20 B samples, 6 exceeded the limit, up to 310 CFU/mL; no E. coli detected, and the one A sample with total coliforms did not recur in B. New machines and filters, lower daily usage, longer standing times, and humid environments correlated with higher exceedance. Disinfection/flush improved some samples but did not eliminate risk; experts advocate boiling water for direct drinking and suggest possible UV sterilization after the post-filter, noting no unified direct-drinking standard exists.

article.articleHeadline: Bacterial Pneumonia Linked to Worse Outcomes in Hospitalized Influenza A
article.articleSummary: In Xi’an, a retrospective cohort at a tertiary hospital evaluated adults hospitalized with influenza A(H1N1) from March 2023–February 2025. Of 453 patients, 290 underwent culture testing (sputum, BALF, or blood). Culture-positive bacterial pneumonia occurred in 41 (14.1%) of the tested group, with Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa each accounting for 21.95% of culture-positive cases; Gram-negative organisms predominated. Compared with culture-negative patients, those with bacterial pneumonia had more severe pneumonia, higher ventilation needs, and longer hospital stays. Exploratory analyses within 48 hours of admission showed higher WBC counts, CRP, and procalcitonin in culture-positive cases. Adjusted analyses indicated discharge hypoalbuminemia strongly associated with culture positivity (OR ~3.0; p=0.003 in standard, ~2.98; p=0.003 in Firth). Associations with chronic respiratory disease were uncertain (p≈0.06). The study notes limitations of retrospective design and non-universal culture testing, urging cautious interpretation.

article.articleHeadline: Bare-handed, with no gloves on, grabbing it... what about the bacteria in canned peaches?
article.articleSummary: Video from a Chinese food processing plant shows workers packing peach segments by hand, without gloves, into plastic cups. The video's authenticity and the plant's identity, manufacturer, product distribution, and domestic import status are unconfirmed. The incident highlights contamination risk from poor hand hygiene in processed foods, especially sugar- or moisture-rich products that support microbial growth. Two pathogens of concern are Staphylococcus aureus, common on skin, which can transfer to food and cause vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and nausea within 1–5 hours, and norovirus, which can spread via contaminated hands or water and trigger acute gastroenteritis with dehydration, hazardous for infants and the elderly. Practical advice includes strict hand and tool cleanliness, avoiding bare-handed contact; if illness occurs, drink boiled water or electrolyte solutions, eat bland foods during recovery, and avoid laxatives. Seek medical care for high fever or bloody stools. Domestic/import status remains unconfirmed.

article.articleHeadline: Multiple Brain Abscesses in Immunocompetent Children Linked to
article.articleSummary: Streptococcus intermedius is a primary pathogen in pediatric brain abscesses, including among immunocompetent children. A 7-year-old boy in China presented with multiple brain abscesses and no prior health issues. A systematic PubMed review identified 42 additional pediatric cases of S. intermedius–associated brain abscesses described in English and French literature, with a male predominance. Importantly, these infections can occur without chronic illness or traditional predisposing factors. Clinicians should maintain vigilance for neurological symptoms in otherwise healthy children to enable rapid diagnosis, timely laboratory confirmation, and comprehensive treatment. The report, published in Frontiers in Pediatrics on 2026-11-16, underscores early recognition and management to improve prognosis in pediatric intracranial infections caused by S. intermedius.

article.articleHeadline: Drug-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae in Livestock Foods Pose Escalating Global
article.articleSummary: Two-decade narrative review identifies livestock-derived foods—especially meat and milk—as major global reservoirs for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)–producing multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, chiefly Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Salmonella. Contamination spans Asia, Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania, with high prevalence in dairy and various meats reflecting production practices and antibiotic use. In Bangladesh, ESBL E. coli is found in raw milk (≈59%), beef (≈57%), mutton (≈43%), chicken (≈30%), and buffalo milk (≈9%); ESBL K. pneumoniae appears in raw milk (20%) and poultry (≈49%). India shows milk E. coli contamination from 1.5% to 37.8% (pooled ≈9%). Pakistan reports beef E. coli at 60%, mutton 32%, chicken 47.6%, with K. pneumoniae in raw milk at 17%. China reports MDR Salmonella in chicken (81.1%) and pork (73.2%). Europe and North America exhibit regional variation with relatively lower retail contamination; surveillance links farm practices to food-safety risks across the globe.

article.articleHeadline: Over 9,000 Hubei Foodborne Illness Cases Reported Watermelon Consumption
article.articleSummary: From 2013–2023, Hubei Province, China, recorded 9,662 watermelon-associated foodborne illness cases, comprising 48.22% of fruit-related illnesses (20,034) and about 4.3% of the province’s 227,099 total foodborne cases. Cases rose from 33 in 2013 to 2,641 in 2023. Geographic spread across all 17 prefectures shows Shiyan (1,318 cases, 13.64%) and Wuhan (1,267, 13.11%) as the top localities; Shennongjia forestry district had as few as 30. Demographically, peaks occur among children under six and adults over 40 (together 66.8%); farmers account for 40.3%. Clinically, virtually all patients had gastrointestinal symptoms (99.35%), with diarrhea (94.52%) and abdominal pain (53.08%). Exposure categories include cold watermelon (47.51%) and exclusive watermelon (32.55%). Etiological confirmation was limited (47/1,676; 2.80%), with norovirus documented in 22 cases. The study uses descriptive national surveillance data to guide targeted public health action.

article.articleHeadline: Multidisciplinary Care Resolves Severe Disseminated Tuberculosis and
article.articleSummary: Qinghai, China documents a single case of a 24-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks’ gestation with concurrent hematogenous disseminated tuberculosis, tuberculous meningitis, and active hepatitis B. Household exposure to pulmonary TB via her sister preceded two weeks of headaches, vomiting, and back pain. CSF Xpert detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis without rifampicin resistance; opening pressure >330 mm H2O; CSF showed abundant nucleated cells, elevated protein, low glucose, and reduced chloride. Chest CT revealed diffuse bilateral miliary nodules. HBV DNA was 1.94×10^8 IU/mL with triple-positive serology; TST and IGRA positive; HIV negative. In ICU, intracranial hypertension was managed by continuous lumbar cisternal CSF drainage, avoiding pregnancy-category C hyperosmolar agents. TB therapy began Oct 10 with isoniazid 0.6 g daily, rifampicin 0.45 g daily, ethambutol 0.75 g daily; pyrazinamide omitted due to GI intolerance. Co-infections included Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and Candida albicans, treated with azithromycin and nystatin. On Oct 15, deterioration prompted escalation of antimycobacterial therapy.

article.articleHeadline: Two Decades of Surveillance Reveal Rising Dengue Burden Across China
article.articleSummary: Two decades of dengue surveillance in China show a shift from sporadic imported infections to a domestic public health threat. Reported cases rose from 40 (2005) to 24,278 (2024), with a cumulative 138,885 cases and 14 deaths across 31 divisions and the Xinjiang Corps. Age-standardized incidence climbed from 0.0036 to 1.6984 per 100,000, peaking at 4.1092 per 100,000 in 2014 (46,864 cases). Joinpoint analysis estimates an average annual percent change of 30.1%. Diagnoses rely on nucleic acid testing; 2008 revisions added IgG/IgM serology, while 2018 revisions recognized NS1 antigen and severe dengue definitions. Epidemics occurred in 2014, 2019, 2023, and 2024. A 2020–2022 decline tracked COVID-19 NPIs and border controls that reduced importation of foreign lineages, with resurgence in 2023. Geographic spread expanded from 31 districts in 2005 to 895 districts in 2024 across 28 divisions; Guangdong accounted for 11 of 14 deaths, and Yunnan showed across-demographic incidence increases.

Health authorities have initiated larval control around homes, fogging, and the deployment of MLO oil in stagnant water, while blood tests for fever patients are being intensified. Hospitals have been instructed to maintain essential medicines stock and to restrict nonessential staff leaves to ensure care. CMHO Dr. Ashok Maharia emphasized mandatory blood investigations for fever cases.

article.articleHeadline: World Health Organization: More than 10 million tuberculosis cases and 1.1 million deaths in 2025.
article.articleSummary: WHO reports 10.6 million tuberculosis (TB) cases and 1.1 million TB deaths in 2025, with progress slower than targets. The global TB incidence rate fell 14% since 2015, far short of the 50% reduction target for 2025; TB deaths declined 35% over the same period, achieving the first mortality milestone of the End TB Strategy about five years late. About 88% of cases are concentrated in 30 countries. Regional trends show Europe with a 42% reduction in incidence, Africa 30%, Southeast Asia 18%, and the Eastern Mediterranean 6.6% decline; the Americas region experienced increases for a fifth straight year. Global TB funding and research remain inadequate, with 2023 funding at ~$1.2 billion vs the $5 billion annual target for 2027. India is highlighted for major strides toward elimination; TB treatment has saved ~86 million lives since 2000. Source: WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Are masks and lockdowns returning? A new COVID variant with head covering; is India under a cloud of concern? Here’s what you need to know.
article.articleSummary: PJ.2.1 is a SARS-CoV-2 variant with 25+ mutations in the spike protein, nicknamed the 'Saltation' or 'Jump' variant. First detected in Ontario, Canada on May 2, 2026, it has since been reported in the United States, Spain, France, Israel, Singapore, Australia, and New Zealand. Mutations enhance binding to the ACE2 receptor, aiding cell entry and spread, but lab data do not indicate higher transmissibility or significant immune escape. There are no distinct symptoms beyond usual COVID-19 manifestations; some patients may experience shortness of breath or altered sense of smell/taste. Overall severity is unclear, though older adults (70+) may be more frequently affected. India has not confirmed PJ.2.1; genomic surveillance by INSACOG and WHO monitoring continue to track arrivals and changes in the variant.

article.articleHeadline: From pet dogs to cats: Understanding the infections that can spread from animals to humans and how to prevent them
article.articleSummary: Dr Subramanian Swaminathan of Gleneagles Hospital, Chennai, explains that living with pets carries zoonotic infection risks, even when animals appear healthy. A prime example is Bartonella henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease and can infect humans when a scratch is contaminated with infected flea feces. Symptoms typically include fever and swollen lymph nodes, appearing a week or more after exposure. Transmission arises from bites, scratches, saliva, urine, feces, contaminated food or water, or contact with an infected animal’s surroundings; insects can also spread pathogens. Preventive measures are crucial for young children, older adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. Recommendations: keep vaccinations and deworming up to date, use veterinarian-approved flea and tick control, dispose of waste safely, wash hands after handling pets, keep litter trays and feeding areas away from food prep, avoid allowing pets to lick wounds or the face, and supervise children. Published 16 November 2026.

He recorded a video of his infected hands that circulated online, drawing praise for his cleanup work. Despite wearing protective gear, direct exposure to dirty water contributed to the infection, which he says began about five days prior to the article; he has since recovered and is reportedly healthy now. The piece underscores persistent river pollution and the broader public responsibility to keep waterways clean.

article.articleSummary: As of November 16, 2026, Sakon Nakhon Province, Thailand, warns residents to be vigilant for mpox (monkeypox). Transmission occurs via close contact with an infected person, especially touching lesions, bodily fluids, or items contaminated with the virus (clothing, towels), and prolonged close proximity. Authorities urge self-care and protecting others to prevent community spread, noting mpox does not spread easily through everyday activities. Symptoms to monitor include fever, headache, muscle aches, and swollen lymph nodes, followed by abnormal rashes or lesions that may start as red spots and progress to vesicles, pustules, and crusts. Lesions may appear on the face, palms, soles, genitals, or anus. If symptoms develop or there is a history of exposure, avoid close contact, seek medical evaluation promptly, and provide accurate exposure details. Do not panic, but take appropriate precautions.

article.articleSummary: Streptococcus suis infection presenting as fever with deafness is rising in Nakhon Ratchasima Province, Thailand, with 76 cases and 9 deaths reported in 2026 as of November 11; four new cases were recorded in early November. Among Isan Health Region 9 provinces, Korat has the highest case and mortality burden. The distribution is concentrated in Mueang Nakhon Ratchasima District, followed by Phimai, Khams Tha Le Sao, Kam Sakaeng, and Dan Khun Thot. The at‑risk groups are older adults, especially 70+, and individuals 50+ with comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, heart disease, or immunosuppression; heavy alcohol use also increases risk. Transmission occurs via consumption of undercooked/raw pork products (e.g., larb, raw pork, blood, nem) and through wounds from handling raw pork. Preventive measures include fully cooked pork, separate utensils, safe sourcing, and protective gear for handlers; seek urgent medical care for fever, severe headache, dizziness, or hearing loss after raw pork exposure.

article.articleHeadline: Zombie fish appear on the Mekong River in Thailand.
article.articleSummary: Zombie catfish with nodules, ulcers, and discolored fins were found in Thailand’s Mekong River, triggering concerns about heavy-metal pollution and seafood safety. Images circulated after 14 November showing Pla khae catfish caught along the Mekong in Loei and Nong Khai. Activist Aombun Thipsuna and local fishermen sent about 60 fish to Naresuan University; six exhibited severe nodules/ulcers, while 30–40 others showed early signs such as red fins/tails or small nodules. Thai monitoring data indicate Mekong metal concentrations rising since 2023; in August arsenic levels at Loei and Nong Khai were 3–4 times the standard 0.01 mg/L. Prior checks found digenean trematode parasites in similar lesions, but a direct causal link to pollution is unproven. An inter-agency meeting on 23 November will coordinate water quality monitoring, seafood testing, and consumer risk assessment.

article.articleHeadline: 'Whooping cough' is a dangerous disease that can weaken infants and put their lives at risk.
article.articleSummary: Pertussis (whooping cough), caused by Bordetella pertussis and spread via respiratory droplets, poses a high risk to infants and young children with immature immunity. Without timely treatment, it can cause severe complications such as pneumonia, seizures, or death. WHO data show rising global activity: more than 150,000 cases worldwide in 2023; the United States records over 15,000 annually, and Thailand has increasing cases, particularly among unvaccinated or under-vaccinated children. The disease progresses in three stages: catarrhal (cold-like symptoms for 1–2 weeks), paroxysmal (repeated coughing fits with a whoop, lasting 1–6 weeks and potentially causing vomiting or breathing difficulty), and convalescent (gradual recovery). On average, affected children cough around 112 days. Antibiotics are most effective within seven days of symptoms; severe cases may require hospitalization. Prevention relies on DTP vaccination at 2, 4, 6, and 18 months, plus boosters for adolescents and adults every 10 years.

article.articleHeadline: Two Plasmodium falciparum Gene Variants Modestly Associate With Severe
article.articleSummary: Plasmodium falciparum cbp1 and cbp2, genes encoding CX3CL1-binding proteins, show non-coding polymorphisms modestly linked to malaria severity in Thailand. In a cohort of 473 clinical isolates from patients with mild malaria, cerebral malaria, or severe malaria without cerebral complications, cbp1 379 C/T (intron near the splicing site) associated with cerebral malaria (odds ratio 1.99, 95% CI 1.03–3.85). cbp2 2306 A/T (3′ UTR) associated with severe malaria without cerebral complications (OR 6.67, 95% CI 1.28–34.73). Parasite density did not differ across cbp1/cbp2 genotypes. Genomic analysis found high conservation: cbp1 had nine SNPs (three coding synonymous), cbp2 had three non-coding SNPs and nine microsatellites, with no coding variants in cbp2. Illumina sequencing of 30 isolates guided broader genotyping by PCR-RFLP and Sanger on 473 samples. Authors call for functional studies to understand how these non-coding variants influence host–parasite interactions and disease severity.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue Fever Knows No Season, Jumantik Also Continues to Eradicate Larvae
article.articleSummary: Dengue Fever (DBD) remains a year-round threat in Jakarta as Aedes aegypti larvae (jentik) are found beyond the rainy season. On 13 November 2026 at 08:30 WIB in Slipi, West Jakarta, Jumantik volunteers from RT 002 RW 002 Palmerah conducted a house-to-house larval source reduction (PSN) drive, forming two groups (~15 houses each) to inspect 35 residences. Three homes harbored larvae. Larvae were commonly found in outdoor plant pots and discarded items, with interior breeding in bathtubs or unsealed water containers. Muhammad Agus Setiawan of Puskesmas Palmerah urged immediate larval disposal and resident education; checks occur at least twice weekly. Volunteers like Nurhikmah (48) in Kemanggisan and Dina (27) in Grogol Utara monitor over 50 homes, focusing on exterior areas and hidden spaces, and intensify efforts if a Dengue case is confirmed. Abate larvicide is used to prevent further growth.

article.articleHeadline: Understanding the Plague: The Role of Rats and Fleas, and How to Prevent It
article.articleSummary: Plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, remains a public health concern. Transmission in humans involves a three-trophic cycle: rats, rat fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis), and the bacterium. Infected fleas bite humans after their rat hosts die, enabling spillover. House rats (Rattus rattus) and Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) are of particular concern due to proximity to people. Historically, the Black Death (1347–1351) demonstrated the disease’s deadly potential. In Russia, flea vectors are pivotal to human risk, but transmission remains unlikely without infected fleas. In Indonesia, plague activity is limited to several districts on Java, with ongoing Ministry of Health surveillance. The most effective prevention is rodent control in residential areas, including sanitation and securing waste to remove food sources. The report also notes other rat-borne diseases, such as leptospirosis and hantavirus, highlighting the need for general environmental hygiene.

article.articleSummary: South Sulawesi, Indonesia, conducted the country’s first leprosy chemoprophylaxis program using single-dose rifampicin for close contacts of newly diagnosed patients. The eight-day campaign ran Oct 21–28, 2026, across 24 regencies/cities and 257 puskesmas (community health centers), targeting 611 individuals as part of contact tracing and transmission prevention. article.articleHeadline: Surveillance Gaps in Indonesia Hinder Early Detection of Emerging Zoonotic
article.articleSummary: Indonesia's viral surveillance remains limited, resulting in substantial under-detection of zoonotic threats despite the country’s status as a global hotspot for viral emergence. The review notes SARS-CoV's multi-decade challenge and argues post-COVID-19 era still demands upgraded monitoring and heightened government and regional risk assessment. Ecological and demographic drivers—vast biodiversity including one of the planet’s largest bat populations, rapid population growth, deforestation, and land-use change—intensify wildlife-livestock-human interfaces, amplifying spillover risk, further shaped by cultural practices and climate-driven ecological shifts. Diagnostic gaps and incomplete visibility across ecosystems hinder timely detection. The study maps priority viral families in Indonesia, including Coronaviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Orthomyxoviridae (avian influenza), and others such as Flaviviridae, Filoviridae, Hantaviridae, Rhabdoviridae (lyssaviruses), Herpesviridae, Poxviridae (monkeypox), Reoviridae, and Hepeviridae (hepatitis E), with reservoir hosts. It outlines opportunities to strengthen surveillance to enable earlier detection of local spillovers, mitigating future pandemics from viral hotspots.

article.articleSummary: Dengue cases in Rosario, Agusan del Sur total 858 with five deaths since January, and 37 active cases as of 2026-11-16. The Municipal Health Office lists cumulative infections by barangay: Sta. Cruz 171, Bayugan 3 169, Cabantao 100, Poblacion 97, Novele 80, Tagbayagan 79, Libuac 67, Cabawan 43, Wasian 33, Maligaya 13, Marfil 6. Active cases are concentrated in Poblacion (11), Sta. Residents are urged to intensify mosquito-control measures: destroy breeding sites, use insect repellents, wear long-sleeved clothing, and seek early medical care for fever, severe headache, or body pains. MHO advisories stress prompt action to curb transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Even a mild fever can push a child into a life-or-death ordeal within 24 hours due to meningococcal disease.
article.articleSummary: Meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) in Vietnam can progress to meningitis and septicemia within hours, with fulminant sepsis causing death in under 24 hours. In Ho Chi Minh City, 5 children have contracted meningococcal disease recently, including a 12-year-old who died from fulminant septic shock and multi-organ failure. Since the start of the year, the Southern region reported 45 cases and 9 deaths. Tay Ninh Province reported two positive cases on Nov 9: a 53-year-old factory worker and a 7-year-old student. Four serogroups—A, C, Y, W—are circulating in Vietnam; groups W and C are particularly virulent. Globally, serogroup W has the highest fatality. A tetravalent vaccine covering A, C, Y, W is available in Vietnam, with evidence of up to 90% risk reduction in adolescents and reduced transmission; it can be given in the first year of life. Prevention also includes hygiene and consulting a physician about vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Colin Carlson, Yale Epidemiologist: "El Niño Will Be Deadly From Swine Flu, WHO Should Declare a State of Emergency"
article.articleSummary: El Niño 2026–27 could cause up to 857,000 heat-related deaths globally, with about 451,000 between June 2026 and February 2027 and roughly 373,000 in October–March, per the Chicago Climate Impact Lab. Regional fatalities include Sahel 66,800 (Nigeria 31,400; Sudan 17,500; Niger 10,000; Chad 8,000); Indonesia 19,300; Philippines/Vietnam/Thailand/Cambodia combined 19,400; India 15,800; Brazil 13,300. The projection centers on heat deaths, but dengue, cholera and other infections could rise concurrently. Yale epidemiologist Colin Carlson and Indiana climate scientist Christopher Callahan urge the WHO to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, akin to Ebola in the DRC and polio spread; they note the 2009 H1N1 swine flu pandemic killed about 284,000. August was record-hot; COP31 reports suggest 2027 will bring more extreme heat, intensifying the global health crisis.

article.articleHeadline: Cardiogenic shock, respiratory failure... due to dengue fever.
article.articleSummary: Two dengue fever cases in southern Vietnam progressed to severe complications requiring ECMO. Case 1: N.K.L., 24, from Ward Vung Tau, Ho Chi Minh City, developed high fever, chest pain, vomiting and diarrhea, then cardiogenic shock from fulminant dengue-related myocarditis with multi-organ failure. He received VA-ECMO to support heart and lungs, improved after a week, vasopressors and ECMO were stopped, and he was discharged. Case 2: L.M.T., born 1991, from Hong Thai Commune, Lam Dong Province, had about a week of fever and cough followed by escalating dyspnea and respiratory failure. He received VV-ECMO at Binh Thuan General Hospital before transfer to Ho Chi Minh City; after four days his lungs recovered, he was extubated, and ECMO was discontinued two days later. ECMO provides temporary life support, not a dengue cure; early evaluation for warning signs is urged.

article.articleHeadline: Warning for Australia as highly contagious disease makes comeback in US
article.articleSummary: United States loses measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years, recording more than 5,400 measles cases in 2026, according to the Pan American Health Organisation/World Health Organisation. Elimination status means no native or ongoing local transmission for at least 12 months. Canada lost elimination status last year. Australia has seen measles outbreaks in Sydney, the Gold Coast and Adelaide, though not at US scale; about 200 cases in Australia over the past few years. Many infections trace to travellers returning from overseas, often Asia. A National Centre for Immunisation Research and Surveillance study says about 6.7% of Australians—roughly 1.7 million—are at risk due to incomplete immunisation. Experts warn Australia is heading in the wrong direction; Professor Brendan Crabb notes measles is appearing more frequently. Some fear other diseases like congenital rubella and pertussis could follow if trends continue.

article.articleHeadline: Urban Expansion Across Sub-Saharan Africa Fuels Complex Malaria
article.articleSummary: Malaria in Sub-Saharan Africa is increasingly driven by urban expansion, with the urban‑peri‑urban interface forming a distinct, persistent transmission zone. A narrative review of 2000–2026 literature (Covenant University, Nigeria) across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar identifies three environments—dense urban cores, dynamic peri‑urban interfaces, and semi‑urban/rural transitions—where peri‑urban areas sustain high transmission despite lower core incidence. In Libreville, Gabon, Plasmodium falciparum prevalence reached 50.9% in semi‑rural and 46.5% in semi‑urban communities in 2023; Bamako, Yaoundé, Lagos, and Accra show similar peripheral burdens due to informal settlements and poor drainage. Bioko Island risk is shaped by travel history to high‑transmission mainland and household wealth. Anopheles gambiae complex adapts to polluted waters; An. coluzzii pupates at 90% in contaminated field water (Cotonou) vs 78.67% lab, and accounts for 54.79% of An. gambiae s.l. in Accra, where 65.34% of breeding sites harbor larvae (drainage ditches 48.21%; urban agriculture 27.24%).

article.articleHeadline: Tanzania: Malaria Fight Gains New Tools, but Elimination Remains Distant
article.articleSummary: Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and Africa-wide, malaria remains a major public health challenge, with 2024 estimates of 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths, mostly among children under five. A New England Journal of Medicine review describes a prevention transition: combining tools to local transmission, strengthening surveillance, and securing financing are essential to move toward elimination. Insecticide-treated nets, once dominant, face pyrethroid resistance, prompting the 2023 rollout of dual-ingredient nets. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention protected 54 million children in 19 sub-Saharan countries in 2024, reducing illness and deaths by 59% at about $4 per child annually. Two vaccines, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M, have WHO prequalification, with 25 African countries introducing vaccination by April 2026 and 62–66% uptake among 3-dose recipients in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, linked to a 32% drop in hospital admissions for severe malaria. Success hinges on tailored strategies, reliable surveillance, and sustainable financing, since vaccines and new tools complement, not replace, vector control and preventive medicines.

article.articleHeadline: Drinking Water: West Africa's Quiet Emergency
article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreaks span six West and Central African countries, with Nigeria reporting over 50,000 cases and 338 deaths since 1 January 2026, driven by flooding that contaminates water sources and damages sanitation. Safe drinking water remains scarce: only 24% of sub-Saharan people have safely managed water; over 400 million West and Central Africans lack safe water. In the Sahel, less than a third of rural residents have a resilient water service; Niger 2024 figures: 47% lacking basic drinking water, 84% lacking basic sanitation, 79% with no handwashing facility at home. Coastal pollution from illegal mining in Ghana threatens rivers; in Liberia, Monrovia’s Slipway residents rely on sachet water and untreated wells. Afrobarometer reports water as a top concern in Guinea and Benin (low public confidence). Calls for at least $440B/year in blended finance; priorities: protect catchments, maintain rural water points, cross-border cholera surveillance, fair tariffs.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in the DRC: 5,471 deaths, the heaviest toll among the 17 outbreaks.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the 17th and deadliest in the country, with 5,471 deaths among 11,197 cases since it was declared on May 15, 2026. As of 16 November 2026, authorities report a record toll surpassing earlier outbreaks; a prior August 1 flare reached 1,117 cases and 702 deaths by April 4, with 295 suspects still under investigation. Symptoms include sudden fever, extreme weakness, and muscle pains, potentially followed by internal or external bleeding; case fatality can reach 90% depending on the strain. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids of infected or deceased individuals. The response is pressured in a country of over 100 million people, with medical teams and international partners intensifying field efforts. Africa CDC had placed ten neighboring or nearby countries on alert, including South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Congo, Burundi, Angola, Central African Republic, and Zambia.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia : Milenge District Records Decline In Malaria Cases
article.articleSummary: Malaria in Milenge district, Zambia, declined from over 13,200 cases in the second quarter of 2026 to about 7,700 in the third quarter of 2026. District Health Director Chiluba Yamba attributed the drop to intensified prevention, including intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (monthly preventive antimalarial drugs during antenatal care) and continued distribution of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs). Preparations for a subsequent mass ITN distribution are underway, with health personnel and community volunteers undergoing training on net use and longevity. Trainers emphasized proper use to counter misuse, such as nets being used for fishing. Ongoing community education and engagement by health workers and volunteers aim to sustain malaria prevention across the district.
